profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a mid-sized international bank after a pilot dashboard based on a dynamical operational-risk model begins misfiring in live use. The model had shown strong forecasting power during historical analysis, but in the last two monthly committee packs it has over-flagged payment operations and failed to highlight a rise in retail onboarding losses after a core-platform migration. The agenda is to diagnose why live forecasts now diverge from expectations, determine whether the issue comes from data handling, model inputs, or interpretation of outputs, and agree on a practical fix before the next Operational Risk Committee. The expected outcome is a short-term remediation plan for the next reporting cycle and a shared explanation of what exactly needs to be corrected.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Quantitative risk modeling, time-series forecasting, operational loss modeling, regulatory model documentation
members.background: Elena trained as a quantitative economist, spent six years in model risk at a central bank, and joined the bank three years ago to build analytically driven operational-risk forecasting tools.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve confidence in the new model ahead of the committee review, avoid a full redevelopment, and show that the issue is an implementation mismatch rather than a flaw in the model design.
hidden_assumptions: A 'loss event' in the model means a consolidated underlying incident after duplicate accounting entries and recoveries are grouped together.
When people refer to 'the Q4 back-test,' they mean the frozen training extract used in December before year-end restatements and reopened cases were loaded.
The 'control-effort adjustment' should only use process-level remediation actions that have explicit effective dates and owner sign-off.
If the model is 'stable enough' for the committee, aggregate 90-day loss forecasts by business line should stay within the expected calibration band even if individual process rankings move around.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.role: Operational Risk Reporting and Systems Lead
members.expertise: Loss data collection, incident taxonomy, GRC system workflows, management reporting, committee pack production
members.background: Priya came up through first-line controls reporting, now owns the bank's operational-loss repository and monthly risk dashboards, and is the main bridge between risk data operations and senior management reporting.
members.private_state: She wants the dashboard to stop confusing process owners, reduce manual explanation in committee packs, and ensure the reporting output matches how incidents are recorded and discussed operationally across the bank.
hidden_assumptions: A 'loss event' means each booked loss line in the GRC platform because that is how finance and the committee ultimately see realized losses.
When people mention 'the Q4 back-test,' they mean the version of Q4 numbers used in the January committee pack after restatements, recoveries, and reopened incidents were reflected.

The 'control-effort adjustment' naturally includes enterprise-wide remediation items, training campaigns, and technology releases if they are mapped in the control library to the affected process family.

If the model is 'stable enough' for the committee, the same processes should remain near the top of the heatmap from one monthly pack to the next so that business heads do not see unexplained ranking swings.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a loss event
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the recent rise in 'event counts' and whether the model is reacting correctly to them.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means incident-level events after multiple accounting postings tied to the same operational failure are consolidated into one modeled event.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means raw booked loss lines in the reporting system, where one incident can appear as several entries because of staged postings, recoveries, or split allocations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In operational-risk reporting, both incident counts and booked loss counts are casually called 'events,' and each person works with the version standard in her own workflow, so the shared term feels fully ordinary and does not trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: Which Q4 back-test they are comparing against
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the Q4 back-test' as evidence that the model used to behave better.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the December frozen extract used to fit and validate the pilot before year-end data corrections were loaded.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya is thinking of the January committee version of Q4, which included restated losses, reopened cases, and revised process mappings.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There was only one widely discussed Q4 analysis in each person's part of the organization, so each assumes the reference is unique and obvious even though two materially different Q4 datasets exist.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the model to be stable enough
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the immediate goal is to make the forecast 'stable enough' for next month's committee pack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means aggregate forecast levels and confidence bands should stop drifting materially at the business-line level, even if process-level ordering changes somewhat.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means the process heatmap and top-risk rankings should stop reshuffling month to month so committee members see a consistent story.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both aggregate calibration and visible rank consistency are legitimate notions of stability in a dashboard context, and because the dashboard contains both views, each assumes her criterion is the natural one behind the shared phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the control-effort adjustment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'refresh the control-effort inputs' before rerunning the model.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes this means updating only signed-off, process-specific remediation actions with explicit start dates for the affected process nodes in the model.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya assumes this also includes broad control library mappings such as enterprise training, migration hardening, and shared platform releases linked to multiple process families.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see the adjustment as using the bank's existing controls framework, but one thinks of a narrow modeling subset while the other thinks of the full reporting taxonomy, and the phrase 'refresh the inputs' sounds procedural enough that neither expects hidden boundary differences.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this as drift between live implementation and the validated setup, not a design failure. In the Q4 back-test, using the December frozen extract before year-end restatements and reopened cases, the model picked up the retail onboarding pattern well enough and did not overstate payments. If I anchor us there, I can steer the discussion toward data handling and input refresh rather than reopening the model structure.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. From my side the main issue is straightforward: in live use we're missing the retail onboarding uptick after the migration, while payments is getting pushed far too hard, and that is not what we saw in the Q4 back-test.

turns.inner_thought: What the committee keeps reacting to is the payments heatmap. In my numbers, event counts are up because the platform has multiple booked lines tied to known payments cases, and those are what people see in the dashboard and finance views. For me, stable enough means the visible process story stops jumping around month to month; otherwise I spend the whole pack explaining why a process went bright red again.
turns.utterance: I agree the most visible problem is payments. The event counts there keep driving the heatmap red, even though the business is treating most of that as known cases, so from a reporting angle it's becoming hard to defend.

turns.inner_thought: If the implementation were lining up with the model definition, clusters of related postings tied to the same underlying incident should not be inflating sensitivity like this. And in the Q4 back-test I mean the frozen validation extract, where the clustering logic behaved reasonably. I should keep this at a high level so it sounds like a manageable calibration issue.
turns.utterance: That's exactly why I think the current behavior is off. The payments spike should have been dampened; the model handled clusters of related events reasonably well in the Q4 back-test, so this looks more like something in the live pipeline than a failure of the design.

turns.inner_thought: In the Q4 back-test as I know it from the January committee pack, several payments items were reopened later and split across cost centers, so the event profile in reporting looked different by the time the pack went out. That's probably why Elena thinks Q4 was cleaner than what I'm seeing. Still, if I say it in normal reporting terms, she'll understand the context without us getting stuck in technical detail.
turns.utterance: That may be part of it, but in the Q4 version we used for committee reporting, several of those payments cases were reopened and split across cost centers, so the pattern looked different in my numbers than it did earlier.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want a redevelopment discussion. The quickest credible fix is to refresh the control-effort inputs, meaning the signed-off, process-level remediation actions with clear effective dates for the affected nodes. The post-migration actions in retail onboarding should already be reducing forward propagation in the model if they're loaded correctly.
turns.utterance: Understood. Given the timing, the fastest fix is probably to refresh the control-effort inputs before we touch anything structural. The post-migration remediation should already be taking some of the pressure out of the downstream forecast.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. I'll pull the latest control mappings from the library, including the migration hardening work, the retraining campaign, and the shared platform fixes that were loaded last month. Those are exactly the things process owners expect to see reflected, and if the model still ignores them the dashboard will keep looking detached from operational reality.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do that. I can pull the latest control mappings, including the migration hardening work, staff retraining, and the shared platform fixes that were loaded last month, and get those into the refresh.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the aggregate 90-day forecasts by business line settle back into the expected calibration band, I'm comfortable saying the model is stable enough for committee. I don't need every process rank to stay fixed; some local movement is normal. The key is to avoid any suggestion that the model itself is unfit.
turns.utterance: Good. If we can get the forecast stable enough by next week, I'm comfortable keeping the current model structure in the committee pack rather than opening up a larger redevelopment conversation.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. Stable enough, to me, means the top of the process heatmap stops reshuffling. Business heads don't care about calibration bands; they care that the same processes don't bounce from amber to red and back with no obvious explanation. If that happens a third month in a row, I'll lose the room in committee.
turns.utterance: That's exactly what I need as well. If the output is stable enough, I can stand behind it, but if the top-ranked processes reshuffle again for a third month in a row the business heads are going to challenge the whole dashboard.

turns.inner_thought: Next step: rerun on the latest extract, but benchmark against the December Q4 validation set and with the control-effort inputs refreshed in the narrow modeling sense. If the aggregate behavior comes back into line, I can document this as an implementation mismatch and preserve confidence ahead of the review.
turns.utterance: So let's do this pragmatically: rerun on the latest extract after the control-effort refresh, then compare that result back to the Q4 benchmark and see whether the behavior has normalized.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send over the updated event file from the GRC platform with the latest booked lines and the refreshed controls feed from the reporting mappings. That should line up with what goes into the committee pack, which is what matters operationally. If the rerun behaves better in that view, I can cut down the manual explanation and keep the story coherent for senior management.
turns.utterance: Works for me. I'll prepare the updated event file and the controls feed tonight, and then we can review the revised forecast tomorrow before the committee pack is finalized.
